summary:
Puerto Rico is a United States territory, and the full United States federal framework applies on the island: statutes, executive orders and agency procedure govern entry, documents, screening, federally funded care and federal custody. Puerto Rico's own legislation does not soften that framework; in the area of trans medical care it sharpens it.

United States travel documents record sex assigned at birth, and the January 2025 executive order eliminated the X marker, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents may present a marker that does not match their appearance at inspection. Entry scrutiny is tightened further for one category of traveller: in February 2025 the United States State Department announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

Airport screening follows federal Transportation Security Administration procedure at Puerto Rico airports. All luggage is screened and may be hand-searched. Prosthetics, including breast forms, are treated as medically necessary and are not subject to the three-liquid rule, and medical equipment and prosthetics are admitted through the checkpoint after screening; the National Center for Transgender Equality's rights guide advises packing strategies that reduce the likelihood of an invasive search.

Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, directs federal agencies including the Bureau of Prisons to recognise only two sexes, and federal practice has followed by placing transgender inmates in facilities congruent with their sex assigned at birth rather than their asserted gender identity. The American Civil Liberties Union reported that transgender women had been transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting how many transgender people it holds. Advocates state that the order contravenes the Prison Rape Elimination Act requirement that trans inmates' housing be decided by an individual safety assessment. Federal custody rules govern in Puerto Rico as a United States territory.

In July 2025 Puerto Rico banned gender-affirming care for anyone under 21 and barred public funding for it. Doctors who violate the ban face up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine and permanent loss of their licences. A report on the statute describes it as the most extreme care restriction enacted in any United States jurisdiction, and the Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation has announced plans to challenge it in court.

Violence against transgender people on the island has drawn official response. Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics, and the territory is also covered by the federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. 2020 was the first year anyone in Puerto Rico was charged with a hate crime: Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged after Bonilla confessed that he and Díaz de León murdered two transgender women on 22 April 2020. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over the ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island.
tangentialFactors:
Puerto Rico's sodomy ban was upheld by the Puerto Rico Supreme Court in 2002. After the United States Supreme Court's Lawrence v. Texas ruling in 2003 struck down state and territorial sodomy statutes covering consensual private acts, Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute.

The territory's anti-discrimination machinery has repeatedly stalled. An anti-discrimination bill, House Bill 1725, passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 and would have barred discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, public transportation and public facilities, business transactions and housing; the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved. The 2013 law that did pass, Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013, was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination.

Religious-freedom and conversion-therapy bills have been the site of sustained contest. A 2017 religious freedom bill that would have let public businesses legally discriminate against LGBTQ people was vetoed by Governor Ricardo Rosselló in February 2018. In April 2019 Governor Rosselló announced SB1253, framed as clarifying religious freedom principles, alongside SB1254, a conversion-therapy ban carrying a pastoral exemption for clergy; Johanne Velez Garcia, president of the territory's LGBT council, and allied advocates said the pair would open doors to discrimination and criticised the religious-freedom carve-out as licence to refuse service on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Separately, in March 2019 the pro-statehood NPP caucus in the Puerto Rico House blocked a floor vote on SB1000, which would have banned conversion therapy for minors, despite Senate passage and governor support; Senator Zoe Laboy, a co-sponsor, dissented publicly. Governor Rosselló asked lawmakers to withdraw SB1253 and SB1254 on 13 June 2019 amid sustained opposition, and the similar bill pending after House approval was withdrawn the same day amid protests.

The route to marriage equality in Puerto Rico ran through federal court. In March 2014 the Ada Conde Vidal lawsuit was filed, and four same-sex couples joined it that June, with Lambda Legal and Puerto Rico Para Todas intervening; among the plaintiffs was a former National Guard member, one couple had married in Canada in 2007 and another in New York in 2012.

By comparison with other United States jurisdictions, the 2025 under-21 care ban is described in the source reporting as the most extreme such restriction in force anywhere in the country's states and territories.
localsOnly:
The July 2025 care ban applies to residents as well as visitors. It was pushed through non-public hearings and is deliberately worded so that physicians and affirming parents who facilitate hormone replacement therapy or top surgery risk prosecution. The statute mandates campaigns by the Education and Health departments on the supposed risks of trans-affirming care.

Health Secretary Carlos Mellado's office, identified in reporting as the Health Secretary Ramos Otero, proposed amendments that would have allowed puberty blockers and the continuation of existing hormone replacement therapy; the enacted text did not adopt them and stands as the more restrictive version.

Discrimination protection for residents is narrow. Because Senate Bill 238 was amended in the House in 2013 to cover employment discrimination only, public facilities, public transportation, business transactions and housing remain uncovered by territory law.

Domestic violence protection is broader: in 2013 the legislature passed House Bill 488, signed 29 May 2013, extending domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
No separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections policy, special housing unit or court ruling specific to transgender inmates was located, so the operative rules for trans people in territorial custody are the federal Bureau of Prisons instructions described above.

The outcome of the Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation's announced legal challenge to the under-21 care ban is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

Whether the amendments proposed by the Health Secretary were adopted in any later session, or whether the statute has been amended since enactment in July 2025, is not resolved by the available sources.

Rules governing gender markers on Puerto Rico-issued identity documents, including driving licences and birth certificates, are not covered by this inventory and should be verified separately before travel.
